Question: For each integer \(n \ge 4,\) let \(a_n\) denote the base-\(n\) number \(0.\overline{133}_n.\) The product \(a_4 a_5 \ldots a_{99}\) can be expressed as \(\dfrac{m}{n!},\) where \(m\) and \(n\) are positive integers and \(n\) is as small as possible. What is the value of \(m?\)
Solution:
Use \(k\) for the base so that the factorial index \(n\) remains separate. The repeating block has value \(k^{-1}+3k^{-2}+3k^{-3}\), and each following block is \(k^{-3}\) times the previous one. Since \(k\ge4\), this ratio lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_k
&=\frac{k^{-1}+3k^{-2}+3k^{-3}}{1-k^{-3}}\\
&=\frac{k^2+3k+3}{k^3-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator resembles the quadratic factor of a difference of cubes. Define \(F(k)=k^2+k+1\). Then
\[
k^2+3k+3=F(k+1),
\qquad k^3-1=(k-1)F(k),
\]
so
\[
a_k=\frac{F(k+1)}{(k-1)F(k)}.
\]
All these denominators are positive for \(k\ge4\). In the product, the factors \(F(5),F(6),\ldots,F(99)\) cancel, leaving only the endpoints:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{k=4}^{99}a_k
&=\frac{F(100)}{F(4)}
\cdot\frac{1}{3\cdot4\cdots98}\\
&=\frac{10101}{21}\cdot\frac{2}{98!}\\
&=\frac{962}{98!}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It remains to prove that \(98\) is the smallest possible factorial index. If some \(n\le97\) gave an integer numerator, multiplying the product by \(97!\) would give an integer, because \(97!/n!\) is an integer. But
\[
97!\prod_{k=4}^{99}a_k=\frac{962}{98},
\]
which is not an integer: \(962=9\cdot98+80\). Thus every smaller factorial denominator is impossible. The minimum index is \(n=98\), and the requested numerator is \(\boxed{962}\), choice \(\text{E}\).
